💡 Key Takeaways
  • At some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married?
  • For Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office.
  • Industry observers note that joan listed a few traits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married? What if I never find my person and end up alone?

For Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office. Back then, she says, “a woman who didn’t want a husband was assumed to have something wrong with her.” But her therapist—married with children, yet more open-minded than most—didn’t try to correct her with cheesy motivational mantras or fear tactics about a “ticking clock.” Instead, she asked a different question: What kind of husband would you want, if you had one?

Industry observers note that joan listed a few traits. Someone busy, she recalls saying. Someone deeply absorbed in his own life—his job, his hobbies, his community.

“So you'd want someone intellectually stimulating?” her therapist asked.

According to recent reports, “No,” Joan replied. “I’d want someone who’s never home.”.

It landed as a joke, though deep down, it wasn’t. What came from that session was an almost accidental realization that sounded radical at the time (it was around 1980): “Some people genuinely live their best lives independently,” Joan tells me. Now 79, single, and uninterested in changing her relationship status, she has spent decades proving her theory true.

Recent findings suggest that for much of modern history, women like Joan were cast as anomalies, freaks, or worse: cautionary tales. There’s “the childless cat lady.” The “old maid.” The “lonely spinster.” Singlehood was framed as a transitional phase, a temporary stop on the way to finding the One. Not an end goal, and certainly not a fulfilling one.

But the stigma is softening—and the older, unmarried women of this generation are living proof that a life without a husband isn’t a fallback; it’s a deeply satisfying choice.

It has been revealed that you can see it in the collective fatigue around modern dating (78% of users on apps including Tinder, Hinge, and Bumble reported feeling burnt out, per a recent Forbes Health survey). Young adults in their mid 20s to early 30s (the supposed “prime marriage years”) are having far less sex than previous generations, with sexual inactivity up roughly 50% for women over the past decade. The shift shows up in pop culture too—in particular, the growing appetite for plots that sideline romance in favor of friendship, independence, and chosen families (like in Barbie and Wicked).

It has been revealed that but perhaps the clearest proof is in lived experiences. The several 70-somethings I spoke with for this story have been single for decades—and aren’t wishing they’d done it any differently. If anything, their lives carry a sense of ease and expansiveness. Many describe weekly, laughter-filled girls’ nights and happy hours; solo trips planned on a whim; financial freedom to buy property, adopt pets, start small businesses…literally do whatever they want, whenever they want. A few still date casually, dipping in and out of steamy flings only when it suits them. Others have opted out of romance entirely. “My favorite part?” one 73-year-old woman tells me bluntly. “Not having to bicker or put up with an incompetent man. That’s probably why I’m the least stressed I’ve ever been.”.

Across their stories, there’s no regret or hint of “missing out.” Just single older ladies enjoying where they are—nothing like the caricatures of the bitter man-hater or the desperate, unlucky romantic we’re used to seeing.

According to recent reports, as Joan is quick to point out, “not everyone starts off wanting a romantic relationship and then moves on to singlehood as Strategy B.” It’s a perspective that’s become increasingly common, so much so that sociologist Bella DePaulo, PhD, built a framework (and wrote a book) about it: being Single at Heart. These are women (including herself) who don’t end up alone; they orient toward it as a genuine preference.

“I still smile when I think about the men I dated when I was a very young adult,” Dr. DePaulo, 72, tells me. “But I remember even more fondly how I felt when each of those relationships ended: finally free.”.

In a recent development, the practical benefits of singledom—solitude, strong friendships, fewer relational stressors—aren’t exclusive to unmarried folks. “But in my opinion, couples are never free the way single people are,” Dr. DePaulo states. The difference, she claims, is psychological: the ability to structure a day, a life, or a passing thought without reflexively factoring in another person’s needs or reactions. “A romantic partner is also there in your mind almost all the time,” Dr. DePaulo points out—even if only on the periphery. “That might be comforting for some. But it can also feel a bit unwelcome, as if they’re always considering what their significant other may be wanting or feeling.” Remove that, and your attention and energy become fully your own.

According to recent reports, of course, the ability to choose this lifestyle is relatively recent. For centuries, marriage wasn’t just a matter of romance—women relied on it for financial stability, social acceptance, and a sanctioned path to family, Kris Marsh, PhD, sociologist and author of The Love Jones Cohort: Single and Living Alone in the Black Middle Class, tells SELF. But with greater access to education, careers, and economic independence (along with broader definitions of intimacy, family, and fulfillment), the pressure to couple up has eased. As of 2023, 42% of US adults were unpartnered, according to the Pew Research Center (up from 29% in 1990). And among the non-daters younger than 50, half aren’t interested in a relationship—though enjoying your single status doesn’t have to involve an anti-love attitude.

According to recent reports, “Now, a lot of women are looking for something additive,” Dr. Marsh says. “I’ve heard over and over, ‘I’m already in a very good place on my own. So you can’t be a distraction. You can’t disrupt my peace.’” Though for most, that epiphany doesn’t happen overnight.

Sources indicate that alice Foster, who recently turned 80, is a classic example of someone who followed the cultural script handed to many in her generation: marry young, raise children, enjoy the stability. “It was fine, but I felt like it was never really about me,” Foster tells SELF. “It wasn’t my life.”.

In 1988, her marriage ended in divorce—though what followed wasn’t the loss she had been taught to fear. It was space. Peace. Recalibration. She moved upstate. Went back to school. Built a fresh career in nursing. Slowly, she began constructing a life that finally felt like her own.

“I feel like I’m in my 50s. It’s been so fun,” she reflects. “I love being retired. I love traveling. I love having people visit me. I love not having to answer to anybody. I’ve been single for so long and loving this life so much that, honestly, I don’t want to get tied down.” And that, experts say, is often how it works.

It has been revealed that rather than being a fixed moral stance or a lifelong rejection of romance, singlehood tends to be a lived, flexible experience—an acceptance of being on your own that you don’t always realize you’re choosing until later. Maybe, like Foster, you leave an unsatisfying marriage. You pull back on exhaustive online dating. You decide this is the year you’ll focus on work, hobbies, or travel. Over time, you stop planning life around the possibility of a relationship…and start seeing that you already have the joy you thought only a husband could provide.

Still, a question tends to linger: Are these women actually happy?

Recent research suggests yes—in fact, satisfaction with singlehood tends to increase with age, starting for people in their 40s. Despite cultural progress, there’s still skepticism as to why anyone would willingly stay single. Whereas married people are taken at their word when they claim fulfillment (even though we know that’s not always true), those who deviate face public scrutiny. “They have to be extra strong, exceptionally confident to stand comfortably in their singleness and validate to the world that they are, in fact, thriving,” Dr. Marsh adds—an expectation that flattens single older ladies into either a hyper-independent success story or a pitiable failure, with little room for nuance.

But that pressure can have an unintended effect too. After decades of being asked by society to justify their lifestyle, many simply stop performing. All of the women I spoke with didn’t overexplain. They weren’t defensive. They didn’t seem especially interested in winning me over.

It takes a certain kind of confidence and clarity to stop shaping your life around what’s expected and historically rewarded, and instead follow what feels good, without apology. What you get then, as Dr. Marsh has observed in her research, is a quieter, rarer form of happiness—one that isn’t performed and doesn’t ask for external validation. Instead, it feels much more genuine. It endures.

The availability you can't find at 3 months may have been wide open at 11 months. 3. **Confirm before you transfer.** Check the Turkish booking tool *first*, then move your points. This keeps the process clean and stress-free. If you're willing to be slightly flexible on dates, this redemption is genuinely beginner-accessible — and the payoff, especially for a family, makes the modest extra effort completely worthwhile.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hoor Al Qasimi, one of the preeminent figures of contemporary art in the Middle East, has been named curator of the Venice Biennale's next art exhibition, the Biennale has revealed.

Following this year's edition, which was curated by the late Cameroon-born curator Koyo Kouoh, the appointment of Al-Qasimi, from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), marks the second consecutive edition in which a woman from outside the Western art world has been chosen for the role.

Al Qasimi was born into the royal family of the port city of Sharjah and is the daughter of Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi, the current leader of the emirate of Sharjah.

She has been involved in the Sharjah Biennial since 2003, when she curated the exhibition's sixth edition after completing her undergraduate studies at the Slade School of Fine Art in London. In 2009, she founded the Sharjah Art Foundation, a public art organisation that promotes and funds contemporary art collaborations in the emirate and internationally, including organising the Sharjah Biennial.

Industry observers note that she holds board positions for numerous other arts organisations, including the International Biennial Association, Sharjah Museums Authority, Sharjah Architecture Triennial and University of the Arts Sharjah. She has also curated major exhibitions including the Lahore Biennale in 2020, the Aichi Triennale in Japan in 2025, and this year's edition of the Biennale of Sydney.

Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, president of the Venice Biennale, says in a statement that Al Qasimi's work gives “voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected”.

He adds: “Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people...These are qualities that we feel are particularly close to La Biennale’s vision”.

Buttafuoco, a right-leaning journalist and intellectual who was born and raised in Catania in Sicily, reportedly converted to Islam in 2015, adopting the name Giafar al-Siqilli (“Jafar the Sicilian”) in a reference to the Arab-Sicilian general associated with the Fatimid conquest of North Africa.

Sources indicate that since becoming president of the Biennale in 2024, he has sometimes championed art from the Middle East. Under his watch, Qatar opened a national pavilion at the Biennale last year, making it the first permanent addition to the Giardini, one of the Biennale's two main venues, in thirty years.

In a statement, Al Qasimi says that the Biennale “continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators”, adding that she was “honoured” to be appointed as curator.

Al Qasimi could not immediately be reached for comment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, outgoing Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III reasserted the institution’s independence in a letter to his staff after a leaked document from a Trump aide laid out a sweeping overhaul of its programming and personnel.

“The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in the letter, which the Latest York Times reviewed and first reported. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.” Related Articles Did a Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveal White House Looks to Revamp the Smithsonian? Rep. Jamie Raskin Wants the Smithsonian to Collect and Display Trump's Propaganda, To Teach About Tyranny.

The document, titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan,” was photographed on a laptop that a Trump aide was using on the Washington Metro. As first reported by ProPublica, its 25-item action list includes prepares to dismiss top curators and administrators, among them Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, whom the White House has accused of promoting “radical activist ideology.”.

The proposal also calls for a upcoming permanent exhibit, “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance,” and another on “Great Families of American History.” It envisions a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington at the museum’s entrance, which would fulfill a request Trump made in September.

The plan appears to be a work in progress: Photos show the aide brainstorming additions in a notebook. One handwritten entry seems to read “No X-rated exhibition policy,” an apparent callback to a particularly contentious stretch of Hartig’s testimony, when lawmakers questioned her about images of bondage wear in an LGBTQ history exhibition. On Monday, ProPublica identified the staffer as an associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office behind a 162-page report that accused the Smithsonian of “extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.”.

Sources indicate that A central complaint of the report was what its authors characterized as anti-white bias at the museum, which they stated showed in its promotion of diversity, equity, and inclusion. The report accused one exhibition, “Many Voices, One Nation,” of trying “to convince visitors that illegal aliens are entitled to citizenship, voting rights and ‘belonging’ in America.” (Two weeks after the report’s release, Trump signed an executive order directing that signs be installed outside the museum warning visitors of its “ideological capture.”).

In a recent development, the document glimpsed on the staffer’s laptop laid out new interpretive guidelines for exhibits, including an explicit end to the Smithsonian’s use of a diversity style guide. The Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions would be reviewed, and one show now on tour, “The Bias Inside Us,” would be halted. Grants to “woke third parties,” such as the American Alliance of Museums, would also be reviewed.

The Smithsonian’s online K-12 curriculum would be overhauled to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” The “Becoming US” module on immigration, for example, would be deleted and replaced with a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”.

According to recent reports, the Smithsonian, a network of 21 museums, is structured to operate independently of the White House. It’s governed by a 17-member Board of Regents: the Chief Justice of the United States, John G. Roberts Jr.; the Vice President, JD Vance; six members of Congress from both parties; and nine private citizens. Legally, the Smithsonian answers to Congress, not the White House, but federal money makes up about 60 percent of its budget. Trump proposed cutting that funding by roughly 12 percent for fiscal year 2026, a threat that ultimately went unrealized.

Industry observers note that bunch, who became secretary in 2019, has repeatedly asserted the institution’s legal independence as pressure from the White House has mounted. The administration has demanded that the Smithsonian turn over internal materials and pushed for the firing of Kim Sajet, the director of the National Portrait Gallery, whom Trump had called “highly partisan.” Sajet ultimately resigned. Bunch has drawn similar attacks: a White House aide reportedly called him a “rabid partisan.”.

In a recent development, in a May interview with the New York Times, Bunch seemed to acknowledge that recent vacancies on the Board of Regents had weakened his position, though he still appeared to have the support of a majority of the board. In September, he announced that he would retire at the end of the year.

In his letter to staff on Tuesday, Bunch wrote, “As I have said before, we welcome scrutiny of our work, and even disagreement. The Smithsonian will continue to be driven by scholarship, research and reflection, free from outside influence and in service to the American people.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns.
  • Sources indicate that each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build.
  • Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Sources indicate that each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:.

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

In a recent development, research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of upcoming love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the challenges head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

It has been revealed that significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

According to recent reports, if you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

According to recent reports, you know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

#206158. 5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

📅 19 Jul 2024 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1058 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

📅 19 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship.
  • Recent findings suggest that most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going.
  • Sources indicate that you might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Recent findings suggest that most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

Sources indicate that you might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

To be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

Sources indicate that look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

Industry observers note that “At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

Venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That noted, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

Industry observers note that if someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher says. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

Maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” looks fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

Industry observers note that “In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher indicates, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

According to recent reports, instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds says. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling aims only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

In a recent development, let’s say you mentioned how crucial it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your major day without a hint of apology.

According to recent reports, true friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely shows empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

Industry observers note that ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That said, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds says. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”.

We were genuinely impressed with some of the new AI features in Photoshop 2027, from Generative Restyle to Relight. But just a couple of weeks after its release, the latest version of the industry-standard image editing software is facing a reputational crisis.

It has been revealed that the Fresh York Times has banned freelance photographers from using the app because of a difficulty in knowing when it uses generative AI. That's just one publication, but the news has made a substantial impact, and the significance is clear: people may not be 100% sure when they are or aren't using generative AI to edit an image.

There's an easy solution, but will Adobe want to introduce it?

Sources indicate that the New York Times wrote in an email to freelance photographers that the newest version of Photoshop “utilizes generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to consumers. Their use can result in metadata misidentifying photos as AI-generated.” As a result photographers have been told not to use the latest version of the software.

Recent findings suggest that in photojournalism, it's an ethical issue. Images need to reflect reality, so editing is usually relatively limited. The inadvertent use of generative AI also brings with it the risk of an "AI content" tag on social media, which could lead people to question a report, and could severely damage to the reputation of both the photographer and any media outlet reporting news with an image flagged as AI.

Sources indicate that the most obvious solution would be an AI-off switch. Digital artists, designers and those photographers who want to use generative AI tools in Photoshop could turn it on. Photojournalists, documentary photographers, and anyone who simply doesn't want to use generative AI or risk being shamed with an AI content tag, can turn it off.

It has been revealed that other software developers have done just that. Canva added an AI off Switch last week, and Maxon has included the ability to turn off its new generative AI features in Cinema 4D and ZBrush. It's a simple mechanism that can be flicked on or off at any time, and the gesture helps offer reassurance to those consumers who oppose AI.

The question is whether Adobe will be willing to follow this lead, or if it will fear that a switch would call its direction into question or discourage people from using the AI tools it wants to promote.

Adobe didn't immediately respond to an invitation to comment.

Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that barefoot walks on the beach.
  • Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not fresh, though it is gaining in popularity.
  • Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—massive and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not fresh, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

Recent findings suggest that for some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

“It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” states Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

Recent findings suggest that patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting fresh collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is quickly becoming the preferred method.

Recent findings suggest that “[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” says Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

Industry observers note that this type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” states Dr. Pearl.

Dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

While there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

Sources indicate that this is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

Recent findings suggest that try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

For cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

But will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” notes Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

If you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

If injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a proposal to minimize your pain.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even if you haven't spent every waking hour of the past seven days immersed in the world of Leonida, you've sure seen a lot of the GTA logo lately.
  • According to recent reports, for long-time fans of series, the GTA VI logo is a familiar design with the same core wordmark that's been in use since Grand Theft Auto III.
  • The original Grand Theft Auto logo created by The Designers Republic for the first game's marketing featured cartoonish stars and flames for a '70s vibe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even if you haven't spent every waking hour of the past seven days immersed in the world of Leonida, you've sure seen a lot of the GTA logo lately. Along with the Vice City palette of pastel pinks, blues and sunset oranges, the logo has been everywhere, from developer Rockstar Games' billboards and murals to those GTA VI brand reactions.

According to recent reports, for long-time fans of series, the GTA VI logo is a familiar design with the same core wordmark that's been in use since Grand Theft Auto III. But older readers who have never played GTA might also find it strangely familiar. That could be because it's based on a free typeface that was inspired by a very different kind of game.

The original Grand Theft Auto logo created by The Designers Republic for the first game's marketing featured cartoonish stars and flames for a '70s vibe. It was replaced by a simpler three-letter GTA logo for the second game, in the franchise. It was Grand Theft Auto III in 2001 that introduced the design we know today.

The logo is largely based on Pricedown, a free typeface developed by the Canadian designer Raymond Larabie and published by Typodermic. In his post about the history of the font on the foundry's website, Raymond states his intention was to closely reinterpret Pinto Flare, a display face made for Franklin Photolettering in the late 1960s and best known for its use in The Price Is Right logo.

"I kept the boxy structure and the odd unicase letterforms with swash descenders, but I drew my version harder and more angular compared to Pinto Flare’s softer feel," he writes.

It has been revealed that raymond states he released Pricedown on 30 November 1997. That was just two days after the first GTA came out for windows. And the coincidences don't end there. He says that when the font was later chosen by Rockstar's office in Newly introduced York, he happened to be working as an art director at Rockstar Toronto. His colleagues weren't aware that someone working at the company had designed the font.

Sources indicate that so the world's most expensive video game has a logo based on a free font? And it works: the chunky letterforms with their rounded corners work perfectly achieving easy readability while fitting into the rest of the game's branding.

But it would be a simplification to say that Pricedown is all there is to the GTA logo. Ultimately, Rockstar modified the letterforms and arranged them to make them work as a logo design. The three words of the franchise's name and held tightly in a block that's almost square, the 'r' and 'h' conjoin, and a black stroke provides separation against coloured backgrounds.

An additional touch has been added for each game in the form of the numbering: a pink neon sign-like script for Vice City, tattoo-like blackletter type for San Andreas, the V that recalls US currency design for GTA V.

Considering Grand Theft Auto's satire of US culture and society, it seems fitting for it to have a logo inspired by the identity of one of the country's longest-running TV series (see our pick of the best GTA VI Easter eggs for examples of how the game references pop culture and its own legacy).

Industry observers note that looking for the font? The original Pricedown, now called Pricedown Black is available free for desktop use, and you can download it directly from Typodermic. Raymond later expanded the font into a complete typeface family with other weights. To use those, you'll need to buy a licence. You can find them at MyFonts.

For more on the game of the biggest video game in history, check out our interviews with Rockstar Games' art team on GTA VI's environmental storytelling and the building design in GTA VI.

In a recent development, vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:.

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he notes.

According to recent reports, as Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study demonstrated that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe states this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

In a recent development, “Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe notes. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”.

It has been revealed that nobbe claims WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he indicates.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe states.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising, Los Angeles Times reporter Janny Scott published an essay confronting her own complacency toward the city’s stark inequalities. For years, she’d witnessed the chasm widen between women carrying $3,500 handbags and those wearing trash bags; from her “nice neighborhood where the helicopters don’t come,” she did little to address the disparity. Still, the unrest that followed the acquittal of four LAPD officers charged with beating Rodney King seemed to have broken through the collective apathy. Angelenos, she wrote, were suddenly talking about “things that matter”: race, guilt, poverty, urban policy, to name a few. Despite history offering little reason for optimism, Scott confessed to a sense of hope: “I’m nurturing my first illusion.” Related Articles Christie's Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy Piaget's Latest Release Is a Limited-Edition Andy Warhol Camouflage Watch.

Industry observers note that more than three decades later, artist Guadalupe Rosales found a copy of the newspaper containing Scott’s article on eBay. The headlines “Seeing Ourselves” and “Has the Myth Been Shattered?” registered the same discrepancy she sensed between what she remembered as a child growing up in East LA and how the press perpetuated myths about the city’s seeming collectivity. Rosales was 11 years old in 1992, and she has a distinct memory of her mother rushing the family home from school as smoke stained the usually sun-drenched California sky. As an adult, Rosales has amassed an archive of clippings, photographs, and other ephemera of Chicanx youth culture—much of it crowdsourced through social media—that serves as both a bulwark against that dissonance and a counter to historical erasure and amnesia. “I’m not looking for answers,” she told ARTnews. “But for some kind of physical proof that things really happened, that they’re not just in our memories.”.

Rosales’s 2024 sculpture Has the myth been shattered encases that infamous yellowed newspaper in a nearly six-foot-tall aluminum frame fitted with a two-way mirror, illuminated by colorful LED lights. Though it resembles a doorway, the work offers no passage; instead, viewers face their own reflections superimposed over the 1992 text, along with photographs of palm trees and police. The temporal distance between then and now collapses onto a single plane, leaving Scott’s question perpetually suspended in the present.

Sources indicate that the work also lends its title to a just-opened exhibition at the Broad in downtown LA. Organized by assistant curator Jen Vanegas Rocha, the presentation brings together works by more than a dozen artists spanning six decades. Recent acquisitions by Rosales and Hank Willis Thomas appear alongside art by Andy Warhol, Barbara Kruger, Glenn Ligon, and Robert Longo, among others. Across prints, paintings, drawings, sculpture, and tapestry, artists appropriate text and images from various forms of public record, drawing attention to the ways media shapes perception of major sociopolitical events. Seen together, the works undermine the assumption that exposing injustice inevitably leads to redress. “There are echoes of the present in the past,” Willis Thomas mentioned. “So is the past present or is the present past?”.

The Broad’s founding director, Joanne Heyler, sees that unease as central to the exhibition’s timeliness. “The notion of a linear progression of change unfolding in a dependable, escalating way,” she said, is “becoming harder and harder to believe in.”.

Consider the oldest work in the show, Andy Warhol’s Race Riot (1963), in which police dogs attack Black civil-rights demonstrators in Birmingham, Alabama. In 2026, the decades-old image calls to mind the police response to the 2020 protests following the murder of George Floyd, as well as the more recent pro-Palestine and anti-ICE demonstrations nationwide, in which protestors were often battered and tear-gassed. Warhol lifted the photograph directly from a visual essay by Charles Moore in Life magazine, translating the confrontation into a monochromatic silkscreen. Adopting the incendiary rhetoric of contemporary news coverage, he labeled the peaceful demonstrators “rioters.” Race Riot reflects the artist’s own reckoning with the contradictions at the heart of American life: His obsession with celebrities and mass consumption give way to the sensationalized images of death and violence that belie it, like the mangled cars and electric chairs that also feature in his “Death and Disaster” series. Viewers are left to consider whether the relentless circulation of violence sharpens public outrage or gradually dulls our empathy.

Industry observers note that for Willis Thomas, Warhol’s Birmingham silkscreen paintings function as “postcards to the future.” By transforming them from documentation to works of art, Warhol has made a case for their continued relevance. Nearby, Willis Thomas’s photo-based Black Survival Guide, or How to Live Through a Police Riot (2018) revisits the same era to recover another history largely omitted from public memory. While researching the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, he discovered a typewritten pamphlet offering practical advice to Black residents of Wilmington, Delaware, during the nine-month National Guard occupation in 1968. Onto retroreflective vinyl, Willis Thomas printed excerpts from the pamphlet—advice on how to staunch bleeding or communicate during a power outage, for example—atop archival News Journal photographs of confrontations between armed soldiers and the city’s Black communities. Installed in a darkened gallery, the black-and-white images are invisible until a flash of light illuminates them. Rather than merely encountering the past, the audience actively aids in its recovery. “In some ways the observers become the researchers,” he stated.

Sources indicate that histories of state-sanctioned violence and resistance movements similarly converge across a nearly eleven-foot-wide canvas in Mickalene Thomas’s 2021 mixed-media painting The Charnel House (Resist #5). Reworking Picasso’s 1944–45 masterpiece of corpses heaped beneath a table made in response to news footage of liberated Nazi concentration camps, Thomas collages photographs and placards from the Civil Rights and Black Lives Matter movements with the modernist’s fragmented anatomical forms. A poster advertising the Black Panther Party’s free breakfast program appears beside a portrait of Angela Davis and the names of Freddie Gray and Alton Sterling, both killed during encounters with police. Here, grief and trauma are paired with resistance and community building.

In a recent development, the language of dissent assumes a subtler register in Ligon’s Narratives (1993), a suite of nine sepia-toned etchings that mimic the ornate typography and florid prose of 19th-century slave narratives. Ligon replaces accounts of enslavement and escape with details from his early education at a predominantly white private school, his desire for other men, and the circumstances of his career as an artist. In his hands, a literary form that freed Black people used to demonstrate their humanity becomes a medium for contemporary self-portraiture and self-determination.

Museums, of course, too, play a role in shaping public records. Over the past five years, the Broad has acquired work by 26 artists previously unrepresented in its collection, many of whom are of a younger generation and, like Rosales, actively working in LA. Heyler sees these acquisitions as part of an ongoing effort to better reflect the multiplicity of the communities that surround the institution. “We’re not telling one story but many,” she noted. “We’re always striving to strengthen the connective tissues between them.”.

The exhibition offers an opportunity to showcase many of the newly acquired artists and to extend an art-historical conversation that Heyler traces to exhibitions like “A Forest of Signs: Art in the Crisis of Representation,” a landmark 1989 survey at the Museum of Contemporary Art, just across the street. Bringing together works by 30 American artists, from Jeff Koons to Jenny Holzer, that show examined the unstable boundaries between reality and representation in an increasingly media-saturated society. But the terrain has evolved, Heyler noted. Where artists of that period often exposed the ideologies concealed by authoritative and commercial imagery, audiences today, immersed in social media and generative AI, navigate what she called a “stew of falsehoods and truths.”.

Even so, curator Vanegas Rocha hopes her exhibition inspires something more generative than cynicism, in which artists can be seen as the “architects of better futures.” She locates the potential for systemic change in the power of an individual aesthetic encounter. “It can teach you about the world, about others, about yourself,” she noted. “That single moment can have a ripple effect, leading to a collective difference.” Rosales, likewise, hasn’t relinquished hope. Citing José Esteban Muñoz’s 2009 queer theory book Cruising Utopia, she described hope as an ever-receding horizon that we must continue to endeavor toward. “We are a people that don’t give up,” she said, noting that her mother also took her to protests from an early age. “Standing up for each other, even when you don’t see it right away, does pay off.” Progress, she suggests, may not be linear or inevitable, but that doesn’t make it an illusion. In her mirror, the unresolved question—“Has the Myth Been Shattered?”—is cast back onto the people who might yet determine the answer.

Industry News: What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one glitch keeps coming up: the side effects.
  • It has been revealed that to be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet.
  • Recent findings suggest that but if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one glitch keeps coming up: the side effects. As key as hitting your daily fiber goal is, your body doesn’t always make doing so easy. Fiber is difficult for your digestive system to break down and has to be handed off to bacteria in the colon instead (which is kind of its point), so piling on too much too fast can result in a barrage of painful, awkward, or inconvenient digestive symptoms—bloating, gas, stomach cramps, the whole nine yards.

It has been revealed that to be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet. “Even with fiber becoming a growing trend, people still greatly underestimate its importance and, also, just how many ways it benefits the human body,” Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. You’re probably familiar with fiber’s ability to keep you full, stave off constipation, and support gut health, but it wears plenty of other hats too, like lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol and stabilizing your blood sugar (not to mention reducing your risk for a slew of diseases in the long run). In fact, overlooking fiber is one of the top nutrition mistakes people make, according to experts.

Recent findings suggest that but if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you. In fact, it’s a complaint that Lisa Ganjhu, DO, a gastroenterologist at NYU Langone Health, hears all the time at work: “I have a lot of patients that will say ‘I ate more fiber, and now I’m really bloated and crampy,’” she says. Thankfully, there’s a way to curtail those disagreeable side effects so you can (comfortably) continue your fiber journey: a strategy Nielsen calls fiber training. Here’s what that involves, and how to start developing those “muscles.”.

In a recent development, fiber training is exactly what it sounds like: training your body to handle fiber better. It’s all about “slow, consistent increases in fiber to help you build your tolerance…while minimizing the potential symptoms,” Nielsen claims.

You can think of fiber training kind of like preparing for a race. “In much the same way that you wouldn’t go out and run a marathon tomorrow if you haven’t run a mile before,” you need to work your way up to a high-fiber diet, Nielsen states. Similarly, Dr. Ganjhu compares it to a weightlifting regimen. Rather than lifting 50-pound weights right off the bat, “you kind of have to adjust slowly,” she says. “You start off with 10. When that becomes easy, you go to 20, then you go to 30”—and so on.

Fiber training is especially critical if you’re constipated at the outset, as many people are, according to Nielsen. Even though fiber can help prevent and alleviate constipation, too much at once can actually make an existing problem worse by overwhelming your gut. “When you add a ton of fiber to an already backed-up system, it’s kind of like a bottleneck on the highway,” Nielsen notes: If you try to shoehorn four lanes into one, you’re going to end up with a jam on your hands.

Industry observers note that now that you know fiber training entails steadily increasing your fiber intake, you’re probably wondering what that looks like on a more practical level. Before we share specifics, some context for how much fiber you actually need might be helpful. Per the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, women should aim for 28 grams of fiber daily from ages 19 to 30, 25 grams of fiber daily from ages 31 to 50, and 22 grams of fiber daily starting at age 51, though some experts recommend even more—a helpful set of parameters if you’re not sure where to start.

While the ideal amount of fiber to add to your diet while fiber training can vary from person to person depending on health needs (like a constipation issue), most people are “looking at [adding] probably three to five grams at a time,” Nielsen says.

With that in mind, you’ll want to choose a food that has a fiber content in that ballpark—say, an apple (around four grams of fiber), a half-cup of chickpeas (around five grams of fiber), a tablespoon of chia seeds (around five grams of fiber), or two tablespoons of ground flax (around four grams of fiber)—and eat a serving every single day until you feel like your body has adjusted (read: you’re not experiencing any additional bloating, gas, or other GI side effects). This process typically takes around five to seven days, according to Nielsen, but everyone’s digestive system is different, so don’t worry if you need more (or less!) time. “It really is about listening to your body and individualizing the rate at which you increase,” Nielsen says. “You have to follow your symptoms and go slow,” Dr. Ganjhu agrees.

Then, you can tack on another dose—like a second apple, a full cup of chickpeas, two tablespoons of chia seeds, or four tablespoons of ground flax. Continue increasing your fiber intake in these increments (and at this pace) until you’ve hit your daily fiber goal. If you’re a 35-year-old woman starting from scratch, reaching 25 grams of fiber—the recommended daily amount for that age—would take around five five-gram doses, six four-gram doses, or eight three-gram doses, for example.

Industry observers note that people who are constipated may want to specifically fiber train with foods that are low in FODMAPs—fermentable carbohydrates particularly hard on sensitive stomachs—according to Nielsen. Like we said above, increasing your fiber intake when you’re backed up can, well, backfire, so low-FODMAP foods are more likely to be a safe bet than their high-FODMAP counterparts. Kiwis, which contain four grams of fiber in a two-fruit serving, are an especially strong option if you fall into this category (and they’ve even been specifically studied as a dietary constipation treatment), Nielsen states. Similarly, she adds, a gentle fiber supplement like Metamucil, which is made from psyllium husk, also “provides a lot of the benefits, but tends to be less irritating to a troubled system.”.

According to recent reports, another tip: If you’re constipated, make sure to drink plenty of water as well (though the oft-referenced eight-glasses-a-day requirement is something of a myth!). Because fiber needs water to work its stool-softening magic, insufficient fluids could leave your bowel movements hard and dry, exacerbating the problem.

Whatever fresh fiber sources you choose, taking this slow-and-steady approach should help ease the transition to a higher intake. “If you’re someone who doesn’t eat a lot of fiber and all of a sudden you start eating 30 grams of it, the colon is just not going to know how to manage that efficiently,” Dr. Ganjhu indicates. But by leveling up little by little? You can heighten that “colonic fitness”—and sidestep the worst of the awkward stage.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets.
  • Recent findings suggest that protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant!
  • And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Recent findings suggest that protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

In a recent development, supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Recent findings suggest that some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:.

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

It has been revealed that what you blend your protein powder with can make a significant difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

  • Schmidt has been at the Brücke-Museum since 2017 and has orchestrated many exhibitions, including Escape into Art?
  • It has been revealed that schmidt was chosen out of 97 candidates who applied for the position.

Recent findings suggest that lisa Marei Schmidt, the director of the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, is leaving her post to take over as director of the Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern, Switzerland, starting August 1, 2027. She will also chair the management board of both institutions and be responsible for their artistic direction. The Renzo Piano-designed Zentrum Paul Klee holds the world’s largest collection of works by Klee, while the Kunstmuseum Bern is Switzerland’s oldest fine art museum.

Schmidt has been at the Brücke-Museum since 2017 and has orchestrated many exhibitions, including Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019), Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22), and Confiscated and Forgotten: The Female Artists Targeted by the Nazi ‘Degenerate Art’ Campaign, which opens April 30 to July 25, 2027. The Berlin museum is right now exhibiting Swedish Modernism until February 28, 2027, with a focus on the artist groups De unga (The Young Ones), De åtta (The Eight) and the Gothenburg Colorists. “To me, museums are places where art and people meet. They provide space for encounters, newly introduced perspectives and dialogue across society,” said Schmidt, in a statement on Thursday. “I very much look forward to getting to know the two remarkable institutions, the teams and the people in the City and Canton of Bern. Together, I hope to build on the Kunstmuseum Bern’s and Zentrum Paul Klee’s distinctive qualities and shape their future development.” Related Articles Artist Tracey Rose Accuses Swiss Museum of Censoring Video Referring to 'Muslim Holocaust' Art Recovered in $400,000 Colorado Theft, Portland Museum Picks Architects for $100 M. Expansion, and More: Morning Links for January 10, 2023.

It has been revealed that schmidt was chosen out of 97 candidates who applied for the position. Jonathan Gimmel, president of the umbrella foundation of Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee, said in a statement that Schmidt brings “remarkable professional expertise, international experience and a deep understanding of people” as she shapes the next “development phase of our museums.”.

Before joining Brücke-Museum, Schmidt was a research trainee at Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen and a curator at the Hamburger Bahnhof from 2012 to 2017. She studied art history and modern German literature in Marburg, Amsterdam, and Berlin before graduating from the Royal College of Art.

Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility.
  • Recent findings suggest that the appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol.
  • That role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a new reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

Recent findings suggest that the appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”.

That role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”.

It has been revealed that but is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Sources indicate that our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a big deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

Beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson notes. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”.

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial issues that occur with age, Dr. Molina says. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”.

Sources indicate that as with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson notes. It’s also extra important to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

In a recent development, there’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she notes—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.
