Latest Update: Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.
  • The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
  • It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum shows today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

With The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh states, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused New Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the problems that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

Sources indicate that “I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”.

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

Sources indicate that the exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is currently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she says has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she mentioned.

The Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo‘s pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.

The 20×20 series, released to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we’ve seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a major impact on the next 20.

With just 10 years between the start of their practices, Escobedo and Lanza Atelier represent two crests on a new wave of Mexican architecture that has brought regional references to the world stage and made adventurous but sympathetic interventions at home in Mexico City.

Escobedo was one of Lanza Atelier’s Alessandro Arienzo’s teachers at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and he and partner Isabel Abascal cite her as an inspiration whose success with kindred ideas has given them the confidence to pursue their vision.

They are becoming known for distilling complexity down to simple and pure gestures, whether in the appropriately snaking crinkle-crankle walls of their Serpentine Pavilion, inspired by the English countryside, their Cancun house with materials and forms drawn from sea snail shells, their Re-Source exhibition design that visitors could take home, or their hierarchy-challenging Family of 4 chairs, prompted by the arrival of their second son.

For Escobedo’s part, she identifies Arienzo and Abascal’s dedication to concept and process, which involves extensive research and testing, as key to their strength.

“Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous,” said Escobedo. “They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play that makes their architecture both thoughtful and joyful.”.

The Lanza story began in 2015, with toilets. Arienzo was approached by a client who, nearing the end of their bike path development in Mexico City, realised that they needed public bathroom facilities along the route. Arienzo suggested to Abascal, originally from Madrid, that they work on together on the project.

Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous. They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play.

Rapidly, their collaboration turned one of architecture’s humblest structures into a nexus for meaning and care.

“We were exploring the scarcity of means and materials, but also the boundaries between inside and outside, and how to make something very simple like a toilet become something larger, like a meeting point and a resting space,” stated Abascal.

“And also how to plan for the future of public architecture that might not be very taken care of or maintained by combining landscape and construction.”.

The finished project features semi-open structures built from concrete blocks and filled with planting, creating a network of shaded resting points along the exposed track.

From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza. Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since].

Bamboo trees loosely divide the male and female toilets, but they share common sinks – a feature that Lanza Atelier pushed for as part of their vision for a space of respectful coexistence between all consumers.

“It came out really naturally and fun, and simple,” mentioned Arienzo. “That first interaction made Lanza happen because we needed to build a manufacturer after that.”.

The nature of the collaboration pushed them to establish a distinct language from the get-go, adds Abascal.

“From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza,” she mentioned.

In a recent development, “Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]. We explored so many different options, and we were so opinionated about how it should be. We very rigorously really gave all the importance to designing a toilet.”.

As Escobedo identifies, Lanza Atelier’s work has a remarkable sense of play considering it lacks the colour, ornamentation or usual curlicues that would prompt association with the word.

Their use of materials is almost austere, in the sense that many of their projects have seen them hone in on just one material and push it to its limits, as in the local Sienna bricks of their Serpentine Pavilion.

According to recent reports, arienzo characterises this “extreme” approach as being “maybe a phase” more than a signature of the studio’s work. Instead, the key feature is how they arrive at the choice.

It has been revealed that “We pick materials because of where the project is or what we have close to the site,” Arienzo stated. “We analyse what’s the best or least aggressive way to build [in that place], because, we always say, building is really violent.”.

Using fewer materials also allows them to focus more on questions of space, and makes it easier for their pavilions and installations, often demountable as a matter of principle, to find a second life.

“The main problem is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract,” stated Abascal.

The main matter is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract.

That’s where the playfulness comes in, the designers identify, allowing them to dig into various elements, flip them, manipulate them and be curious about them.

“That, I think, is the playground,” adds Arienzo.

When asked what qualities each of the duo brings to the table that makes their work together so strong, Arienzo is initially flippant.

“I’m the bad cop,” he says with a smile.

But when the duo finally answers seriously, their responses do seem to reveal something about the alchemy going on behind the scenes.

In a recent development, “I used to call Alessandro’s gaze towards the world ‘the laser eye’,” said Abascal. “He is always pointing things out to me – mostly in our everyday lives, it’s things that the city creates and produces informally, but his laser eye applies to every context.”.

“And it’s not only something visual but has to do with how things are and are put together and solved.”.

For his part, Arienzo describes Abascal as the powerhouse behind Lanza’s ideas and concepts.

“I think she gives a lot of meaning to the projects,” said Arienzo. “I think without this, I would just do soulless stuff. She connects the work with history, with literature, with art.”.

Recent findings suggest that lanza Atelier’s slate presently includes a house in LA to replace one destroyed by the wildfires, several projects in Mexico City and the design for the Expanded Tradition exhibition on contemporary Mexican craft at Qatari museum M7. When we speak, Abascal is on her way to the Canary Islands to conduct research on their architecture for migrant pregnant mothers. It’s a patchwork that is idiosyncratically Lanza.

Neither Arienzo or Abascal seems to be the type to have a 10-year proposal – asked about professional goals, Arienzo replies that they’re more orientated towards taking better care of themselves and their children – but they identify housing, particularly collective housing, as the type of architecture they most want to work on.

They hope to do it within a global industry that demolishes less and values what’s already built more, and that learns from the original “sustainable architecture” of vernacular construction in places like Mexico.

The country has been in the spotlight in the last few years as one of the few in Latin America with a progressive government, and one whose president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has frequently had to stand her ground against its northern neighbour.

Asked about whether government policy has had any positive effect on architecture and related industries at home, Abascal and Arienzo’s good cop and bad cop come out.

“From architects of the older generation, our generation and the younger generation, I can feel a sense of optimism,” remarked Abascal.

“I feel a sense of doing nothing,” remarked Arienzo. “Claudia is way better than what there was before; I’m a leftie. But I think there should be many more competitions around housing in the city.”.

Both say they would like to see more public competitions in place of private developments, and that they would eagerly enter.

In a recent development, “Mexico City’s downtown is beautiful and it’s almost empty,” said Arienzo. “There isn’t a lot of density. I think it should be much more about that. Housing is a substantial problem and will be forever for these big cities.”.

According to recent reports, there is an ideal future for the architects, then. It’s one that would see the urban landscape of their home city benefit from the respect, creativity and serene beauty that is the Lanza calling card.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.
  • Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a fresh kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Jim Stephenson.

Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN.

Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.

Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a fresh kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.

Meanwhile, the design was required to be an expression of the interests and experiences of its clients – designer Fabiane Lee-Perrella, television producer Robin Lee-Perrella and their two sons.

“The atmospheric side of the brief was to somehow encapsulate the clients’ diverse visual tastes and architectural memories from their pasts,” CAN founder Mat Barnes told Dezeen.

“This resulted in the eclecticism of the project; one that is very personal to the clients.”.

Visual references given to CAN included modernist Brazilian architecture projects such as Lina Bo Bardi’s SESC Pompéia in São Paulo, as well as industrial architecture, David Hockney paintings and Moroccan riads.

The resultant design inspired the project’s name, House Tropicália, which nods to the late 1960s Tropicália movement that celebrated bold ideas and rebelled against accepted norms.

“We reject the idea that a project needs to be driven by a single, homogeneous idea or material,” noted Barnes.

“Instead, we celebrate the complexity, diversity and even contradiction inherent in our clients’ tastes and design references,” he continued.

“We see these different influences not as competing ideas, but as an opportunity to create something individual and ultimately more meaningful.”.

The focal point of the project is its highly unique rear elevation, with features including two towers of engineering drainage tubes, which break through a red-steel canopy that extends over the patio.

Meanwhile, bright blue and red fibre-cement panels decorate its elevation, alongside portions of textured raked render and exposed concrete, punctured by irregular shapes.

Details also include a metal sawtooth roof at first-floor level, alongside a bright yellow screen facing the neighbouring property to prevent overlooking.

Finally, at ground level, a full-width set of doors open onto a patio with a winding perimeter, referencing the designs of Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx.

“It brings together a mix of materials, forms and ideas drawn from the huge range of references the clients shared with us,” stated Barnes. “I think it captures the character and personalities of the clients brilliantly.”.

It has been revealed that inside, the back half of the ground floor has been rearranged to maximise its connection to the rear garden. This is where the new open-proposal kitchen, dining and living space is positioned.

Meanwhile, at the front of the ground floor, the studio has created a secondary dining area and living space, and a children’s playroom in the original lounge.

In a recent development, above, a void on the north side of the first floor has been filled to add a main bedroom suite, complete with an ensuite and roof terrace. Another bedroom has also been added.

The roof terrace has a walk-on, diamond-shaped skylight, which sits directly above the dining table.

Interior finishes echo the eclecticism of the exterior, with a bold mix of colours, materials and textures. This includes exposed steel joists and trusses, and a colourful timber kitchen with contrasting black tiles.

Walls of ceramic tiles on the ground floor have shell-like forms, handmade by Fabiane Lee-Perrella with glazing that shifts from pink to blue hues.

A microcement floor runs throughout the ground floor and incorporates pebble inlay that evokes a river and is a nod to the water feature at SESC Pompéia.

CAN hopes the project will highlight the importance of challenging the “established or standard way of doing things in a particular city or context”.

“We think it’s vital to look beyond the usual architectural references and draw inspiration from unexpected places, whether that be sculpture, set design, or even infrastructure,” Barnes stated.

“These disciplines can offer entirely different ways of thinking about space, material and form. Ultimately, it’s about exposing clients to these different ways of doing things.”.

In a recent development, CAN, known fully as Critical Architecture Network, was founded by Barnes in 2016. Its previous projects include the equally bold house extensions Druid Grove and Mountain View.

Photography by Jim Stephenson.

Latest Update: Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

📅 31 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people.
  • But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne?
  • In a recent development, salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”.

But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

In a recent development, salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

In a recent development, adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Sources indicate that adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

Industry observers note that so… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Recent findings suggest that which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Industry observers note that studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

According to recent reports, adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate new cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

In a recent development, adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research highlights that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

In a recent development, though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

  • California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia, USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.

California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia, USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within.

Called InVisible, the project was carried out for Dominion Energy, an electricity provider that was updating the substation in Crystal City, Northern Virginia, just outside of Washington DC.

Atelier Manferdini founder Elena Manferdini, who is Italian and teaches at Sci-Arc in Los Angeles, mentioned that her studio sought to translate the largely functional structure into something more human.

“Critical infrastructure is essential to our cities, yet the Dominion Energy substation is fundamentally designed for machines rather than people,” Manferdini told Dezeen.

“With inVisible, we wanted to explore this dichotomy, transforming a purely functional structure into something meaningful to the surrounding community,” she continued.

“While the interior responds to the needs of machines, the exterior becomes an opportunity to engage with people through color, pattern, and perception, creating a dialogue between infrastructure and the human scale of the city.”.

The substation converts power into different voltages to facilitate the transmission of energy, and the patterns on the sculptural facade were computationally designed to represent that process.

Atelier Manferdini used programming site Processing, which came out of the MIT Media Lab in the early 2000s, to design the colourful tile band that lines the bottom of the structure.

This pattern incorporates 10 colours and tiles of three different sizes, two, four, and six inches across – a reference to voltages – along with “glitches” in the program to create the graphic.

It recalls the Boogie Woogie works of modernist artist Piet Mondrian, which were based on the rhythms of cities.

Above the ceramic pattern, the studio placed massive gridded aluminium panels.

The panels create a ventilated facade system, set at different distances from the exterior walls and stacked where they meet so that sunlight passes through different densities in the gridded pattern, creating a variable light effect.

“The folds catch light and cast shadows, allowing the surface to shift with the time of day and the viewer’s position,” remarked the studio.

At night, the panels are backlit by programmable LEDs.

Overall, the studio noted that it considers the contrast between the monochromatic metal and colour tile patterns a unified image.

“Quiet and metallic above, saturated and granular below, the two bands form a unified architectural composition,” said the studio, with the unseen machines humming with electricity inside.

Other creative takes on infrastructure include a power station in China that Schmidt Hammer Lassen shrouded with steel lamellas and topped with a walkway, as well as a sculptural stormwater facility in Toronto by GH3, a Canadian studio well known for its aesthetic treatment of otherwise overlooked infrastructure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a common assumption that great, adventurous sex is a young person’s game—and with age, it fades into something boring, nonexistent, or just…not worth the effort.

Recent findings suggest that growing up, Karen Bigman fell for the propaganda. “But recently, I’ve done it in restaurant bathrooms,” Bigman, a 62-year-old certified sex educator, tells SELF, before listing off other examples of her scandalous escapades. “I’ve spontaneously met up in hotel rooms when the kids were at home. We even pulled over next to a Duane Reade [convenience store], under the fluorescent lamp, to do it in the back seat of his car.”.

To be clear, sex isn’t always this spontaneous for Bigman. But in both her own life and her work with clients, she insists sex in this stage of life isn’t just happening: It’s getting better. For some, it’s even kinkier—though it’s a reality you rarely hear about and probably don’t want to imagine your parents or grandparents doing.

Industry observers note that the fear that your sex life dies with age doesn’t come from nowhere. Bodies change. Menopause (which typically starts in a person’s 40s or 50s) can bring on a slew of symptoms like vaginal dryness or painful sex. Hormonal shifts can lower libido across all sexes. Energy levels fluctuate—and acting out on desires that once felt automatic may now require more effort, communication, and patience.

Sources indicate that still, none of this has to spell the end of a satisfying bedroom life, according to both sex therapists and real people enjoying sex after 60. Here’s how they maintain the spark—and the small shifts they say make the biggest differences.

Vaginal dryness is one of the most common physical changes that comes with aging—and it’s why many people assume getting frisky in this stage will be uncomfortable or painful.

However, there are plenty of expert-recommended products designed to help, and lube is one of the most effective and underrated. “Put it on before you start and have it at the ready during sex,” Bigman, who also shares her advice on her Taboo to Truth: Life & Sex After 50 podcast, says. Lubricants work by reducing friction, which means less risk of irritation or tearing—and just as importantly, more room for pleasure. For best results, we also recommend applying it not just to the penetrating object (like a penis or vibrator) and what’s being penetrated (your vagina), but also during foreplay—for example, consider sliding between labial folds too. (If you’re unsure what lube to buy, start with this beginner-friendly article.).

In a recent development, in some situations, the matter may not be physical or logistical. It’s that the sex you’re having just…isn’t that great.

“If you’re in a relationship or marriage where sex is not exciting, of course you’re not going to want to do it,” Tammy Nelson, PhD, a 63-year-old AASECT-certified sex therapist, who also speaks from personal experience, tells SELF. “It’s like, if the party isn’t fun, why would you go?”.

Sources indicate that however, one of the many upsides of getting older is acquiring a kind of bluntness your younger self probably shied away from. “At a certain point, you just don’t give a crap,” one 64-year-old woman, speaking anonymously, tells SELF. When you realize life’s too short, you stop worrying so much about how your body looks in certain lighting, how you sound while climaxing, and whether your kinks are “too much.”.

“I was once so ashamed to bring up BDSM—being spanked, choked. You don’t want to scare someone off or be judged,” she claims. But after years of what she calls “vanilla sex,” she discovered a game-changing truth: speaking up is worth it. “I had my first real orgasm—that I didn’t have to fake—at 61.”.

Recent findings suggest that achieving a mind-blowing climax doesn’t require a partner. For the women SELF spoke with, their 50s and 60s marked a turning point in figuring out what made them squirm—where they enjoyed being touched, what kind of stimulation worked, which fantasies excited them—all thanks to masturbation.

“I feel freer now to explore my body,” Shay Martin, 63, who owns Vibratex (the exclusive distributor of the Magic Wand sex toy brand), tells SELF. “When I was younger, I would use my hands manually, but there are so many tools out there [vibrators, anal toys, penis rings, nipple clamps] to help with achieving an orgasm on your own that’s much more intense and lasts longer.”.

Research backs up the benefits of solo play: Not only does masturbation feel great, but it can also boost confidence in your sexuality (something older women are rarely encouraged to embrace) and relieve menopause-related symptoms like vaginal dryness, low sex drive, and mood changes. Once you figure out what feels good, “it becomes a whole lot easier to communicate exactly what you want from another person,” Dr. Nelson indicates—which makes settling for mediocre hookups (the kind you may have tolerated in your 20s) far less likely.

Bodies in their 60s don’t always cooperate the way they used to—and that’s okay.

An aching back and weak knees have made certain positions uncomfortable for Isma, 68. “Standard missionary can be tough, so I usually lie on my side with my husband spooning behind me,” she tells SELF. (Another option experts previously recommended to SELF includes child’s pose, which can give you better control over the positioning of your back. Or, for pelvic pain, you can hop on top to adjust the depth of penetration and keep it shallow.).

Sometimes, Isma claims she uses a wedged, foam pillow under her hips for extra support too. (Yes, there are specialized sex pillows that stay sturdy and don’t flatten out, helping you maintain the right angle without discomfort.) “It’s not as effortless or spontaneous as it used to be,” Isma admits, reflecting on how creating intimacy has changed throughout the years. “But we’ve learned our ways to make it work.”.

According to Dr. Nelson, it’s a common misconception that sex is only “good” when it includes penetration and ends in an orgasm. But expanding your definition—not by lowering your standards but by adjusting them—can keep intimacy exciting and realistic.

That might mean focusing on in-the-moment sensations over outcomes: slower pacing, more touch, less pressure to cum. “He genuinely loves going down on me,” Isma says of her husband, describing a nightly, pre-bed ritual that they have maintained almost every day for the past five years. “I don’t usually finish, and neither does he. It just feels amazing. We always look forward to it.”.

Recent findings suggest that martin has found something similar through practicing erotic massages. “At first I was intimidated, because you hear so much about the decline in libido, pain, lack of newness.” Now, Martin says, the slow buildup and warm oil rubbing throughout her erogenous zones is what she anticipates most.

While sex after 60 may not be the kind of stuff that makes it onto racy TV scenes (for now!), that’s precisely what experts say gives it power: It’s a slow, personalized intimacy built only through decades of experimentation, exploration, and curiosity—the kind that only gets better with age.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body.
  • Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility.
  • Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

Recent findings suggest that when you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Preparing for a Thai massage is simple!

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

It has been revealed that your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

It has been revealed that the ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

This week on Dezeen, we kicked off our 20×20 project, in partnership with Kohler, to celebrate 20 years of Dezeen.

Over the next month, we will reveal the architects and designers who will have the biggest impacts over the next 20 years, as selected by some of the biggest names in architecture and design from the past 20 years.

In a recent development, we started the series with an interview with Harry Nuriev, who was selected by Bjarke Ingels. We then interviewed Lanza Atelier, Freya Tangelder and Swedish Girls, who were selected by Frida Escobedo, Nendo and Sabine Marcelis, respectively.

In a massive week for Dezeen, we also unveiled the winners of the 2026 Dezeen Awards winners at a ceremony in London.

We we revealed the architecture, design and interior project winners, including the Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi (pictured), along with the six designers of the year.

In architecture news, recently revealed images of the White House ballroom drew attention to the huge scale of the project, which many stated “dwarfs” the central residence.

“It notes everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Hilary Clinton on X.

A group of Harvard GSD students also aimed to draw attention to another Donald Trump-backed scheme in Washington DC, by proposing alternative designs to his planned arch.

The two proposals for the planned site of the arch replaced the proposed structure with an expansive pool of water.

Also in the US, plans by SHoP Architects for a supertall skyscraper in Miami, which is backed by Serbian tennis player Novak Djokovic, were revealed.

The 320-metre-tall skyscraper will have a ribbed design and include amenity facilities developed by the tennis player.

In less serious news, American fast-food chain Chipotle released a range of hoodies all with a hidden, insulated pocket for sneaking burritos into cinemas.

The tongue-in-cheek clothing was designed to keep concealed burritos warm to allow for illicit snacking at the movies.

Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a “surreal” house in rural China, a pink commercial building in Mexico and a Cotswolds barn renovation.

Five buildings where the staircase is the facade

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Japanese wedding chapel, an Indian university and a reformed monument to an Albanian dictator are among these public buildings where stairs help to create a dramatic facade.
  • Some, like the MVRDV’s Pyramid of Tirana and Snøhetta’s Shanghai Grand Opera House, were designed specifically to give the public unrivalled access to their architecture.
  • The one thing they all have in common is that they make their stairs the main event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Japanese wedding chapel, an Indian university and a reformed monument to an Albanian dictator are among these public buildings where stairs help to create a dramatic facade.

Some, like the MVRDV’s Pyramid of Tirana and Snøhetta’s Shanghai Grand Opera House, were designed specifically to give the public unrivalled access to their architecture. Others, like the Ribbon Chapel (top image), use stairs to serve as both a viewpoint and a metaphor.

The one thing they all have in common is that they make their stairs the main event.

Prestige University, India, by Sanjay Puri Architects.

More than 460 stepped platforms are arranged on top of Prestige University in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, which was recently crowned education project of the year at the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof gradually steps up from the ground to its full height of 28 metres, reducing the visual heft of the building while providing gathering space for all of the university‘s 3,000 students at the same time.

Drawing on the ancient tradition of Indian stepwells, the staircases are organised around courtyards that help to draw sun and ventilation deep into the building, reducing its dependence on artificial light and air conditioning.

Shanghai Grand Opera House, China, by Snøhetta.

Snøhetta has had a thing for walkable roofs ever since its seminal design for the Oslo Opera House in 2008.

Now, China has received its own take on the theme with the Shanghai Opera House, defined by a giant spiral staircase that curves out of the facade and dramatically cantilevers at its peak.

Much like the slanted roof in Oslo, the stairs were designed to make the building radically accessible to the public – although Dezeen revealed earlier this month that access to the roof is now restricted to paid ticket holders.

Pyramid of Tirana, Albania, by MVRDV and IRI Architecture.

Stairs serve both a practical and symbolic function in MVRDV‘s renovation of the Pyramid of Tirana – a monument built for Albanian dictator Enver Hoxha in the 1980s.

The Dutch architecture studio added steps to the pyramid on all sides to allow people to climb and reclaim the building.

“The first time I saw the Pyramid being walked all over by the youth of Tirana, I was deeply touched by its symbolism and by its incredible optimism,” mentioned MVRDV founding partner Winy Maas.

Ribbon Chapel, Japan, by Hiroshi Nakamura.

Intertwining staircases spiral around the glazed core of this wedding chapel in Onomichi, designed by Tokyo-based architect Hiroshi Nakamura.

The stairs, representing the joining of two people in marriage, meet at the top to create a small viewing platform overlooking Japan‘s Seto Inland Sea.

“Just as two lives go through twists and turns before uniting as one, the two spirals seamlessly connect at their 15.4-metre summit to form a single ribbon,” Nakamura explained.

Hisao & Hiroko Taki Plaza, Japan, by Kengo Kuma and Associates.

This student hub was designed by Kengo Kuma and Associates to resemble a natural landform growing out of the Tokyo Institute of Technology campus.

Wooden bleachers and plants help to conceal the building, which is partially sunken into the ground to retain views of the university’s historic clock tower.

The external staircase that descends into the building is also mirrored inside, helping to blur the boundary between interior and exterior landscape.

Photography by Hufton+Crow.

UK studio ZHA took visual cues from the riverbank site of this national theatre in Morocco when designing its sweeping exterior form, which encases a trio of performance spaces.

Named Théâtre Royal de Rabat, the performance venue for artists and musicians is located between the cities of Rabat and Salé near to the recently completed Mohammed VI Tower, which is the country’s tallest building.

It is the first project completed by ZHA, formerly Zaha Hadid Architects, in Africa.

ZHA revealed its proposal for Théâtre Royal de Rabat in 2010. At the time, the studio’s founder, Zaha Hadid, described the design as “secular”.

“It is uplifting to go into a great space, a heavenly space,” Hadid stated.

“As a performance venue, the Théâtre Royal de Rabat is secular, but it has the capacity to transport the audience to an imaginary space and time.”.

Théâtre Royal de Rabat’s design draws on the topography of its site on the banks of the Bouregreg River, which runs between the two cities.

It contains three performance venues, with its main space being a 1,821-seat theatre, simply named the Auditorium.

This venue is lined with crystal-like, faceted surfaces that the studio modelled on muqarnas – a traditional type of three-dimensional ornamentation found in Islamic architecture.

The walls also double as an acoustic treatment, developed by ZHA with acousticians at Arup “to deliver the highest quality of sound to every seat in the hall”.

The second venue is the Studio Theatre, an adaptable space with retractable seating that ZHA described as “offering a variety of configurations from a flat-floor to a stage with proscenium arch”.

It has a capacity of 250 people and is primarily intended for experimental performances and rehearsals. However, it can also be transformed into a space for events such as talks and educational workshops.

The final performance space is the Amphitheatre, an open-air venue accommodating 7,000 spectators for large public events.

The Amphitheatre and Studio Theatre have not yet been revealed in photos.

Industry observers note that completing the building is a triple-height foyer, described by ZHA as “canyon-like”. It is animated by interlocking staircases that emulate draped, flowing fabric, culminating at a restaurant with views of the river outside.

“Designed as a space for transition and reflection, the foyer encourages curiosity and dialogue to unfold before and after each performance,” noted ZHA.

Théâtre Royal de Rabat uses a mix of air-source heat pumps, ground-source cooling and radiant heating as part of its heating and cooling system, alongside natural ventilation. A rainwater collection system is used for the bathrooms and landscape irrigation.

Elsewhere, ZHA recently completed a performing arts centre in China crowned by a trio of swooping, interconnected volumes informed by traditional Cantonese opera costumes.

Another landmark performance venue that recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Opera House by Snøhetta, which incorporates a giant spiral staircase.

Photography by Hufton+Crow.

Looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

The nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.).

It has been revealed that nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Sources indicate that science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

In a recent development, almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

According to recent reports, older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

It has been revealed that since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

It has been revealed that research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

Industry observers note that in 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Sources indicate that showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

It has been revealed that you can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:.

If you’re newly introduced to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

It has been revealed that don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

Photography by Ori Harpaz.

Miami‘s nightlife scene in the 1990s informed the saturated colours and metallic accents used by local studio Evan Edward inside this apartment in the oceanside city, illustrating what the studio calls its “high-impact minimalism” approach.

Designed for an international family with “personal ties to the city’s storied nightlife era”, the Miami Beach pied-à-terre reflects the hedonistic era that left a distinct stylistic impression.

Industry observers note that “Aesthetically, there was a rawness to the excess and glamour,” Evan Edward co-principal Josh Evan Goldfarb told Dezeen. It was a particularly exciting time for colour and design in general in the city.

“The city was in its early stages of redevelopment – the original art deco glamour and run-down beach patina were a sublime tropical combination.”.

He and co-principal Michael Edward Moirano set about creating interiors that blend contemporary and vintage furniture and decor to reflect “a more seductive side of Miami”.

Industry observers note that in place of a typical South Florida palette of white, beige and turquoise, spaces feature hues of terracotta, burnt orange, burgundy and ochre. These prevalent tones are complemented by flashes of chartreuse, mustard yellow and metallic finishes.

To create a more welcoming space for entertaining, the designers opened the kitchen to the living and dining spaces with the angular island as a central gathering point.

They also connected the foyer to an adjoining unit behind a series of oversized pivot doors.

In a recent development, “The updated floor blueprint completely changed the experience for the clients,” Moirano told Dezeen. “The triangular island is the hub of the space, serving the kitchen and dining banquette area, while also exposing the living area featuring a dramatic view of Biscayne Bay and the Miami skyline.”.

A butter yellow kitchen was paired with richly veined stone countertops that complement the polished-pebble flooring.

The generous island was illuminated by a 1960s five-pendant light feature above, and accompanied by mustard yellow Calligaris bar stools for casual dining and gathering.

Goldfarb was forthcoming about references to personal experiences and spaces.

“One of the references for the kitchen was an artist studio that I visited when growing up in Coconut Grove – the memory is ingrained in my mind’s eye,” noted Goldfarb. “It was just so airy – up in the trees, open windows, patina on all surfaces and artwork and materials strewn about.”.

“The sense of colour and mashup of materials – stone, tile, painted – it’s hard to forget,” he added.

Nestled into a corner, a banquette with olive-toned Rubelli velvet upholstery wraps a circular stainless steel table, while a pair of 1970s folding chromed-steel and leather chairs provide additional seating.

An adjustable lamp by Tito Agnoli for Oluce with a custom shade extends from the wall to hang over the table.

The mellow tones of the kitchen were contrasted by the fiery orange-red of the pivoting foyer doors – a hue that reappears in a bold artwork above the bed in the otherwise neutral-toned primary bedroom.

Metallic accents are dialled up in the powder room where a silver metal mosaic clads the walls and metallic zellige tiles cover the floor.

Moirano described it as a “very sexy disco-inspired discovery off the foyer”.

“The result is a small but impactful space that captures the project’s more theatrical influences through materiality rather than overt decoration,” the studio mentioned.

The team describes the project as an example of its “high-impact minimalism, in which architectural restraint provides a framework for distinctive materials, collectible furnishings, and unexpected moments of visual interest.”.

Located on a barrier island along South Florida’s Atlantic Coast, Miami Beach is renowned for its 1920s art deco architecture and more recent influx of luxury hotels.

Another apartment, on the city’s famous Ocean Drive, was renovated by MW Works to include tropical hardwood and sand-coloured plaster.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

What $10,000 grows to at different rates over 30 years — the rate difference matters more than you think.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 6% annual return.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 8% annual return.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 10% annual return.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Future value (FV) is the projected worth of an investment at a specific point in the future, based on an assumed rate of growth. It answers the most practical question in investing: "If I invest this money today, what will it be worth in 10, 20, or 30 years?".

Future value calculations rest on compound interest — the principle that your returns earn their own returns over time. Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest "the eighth wonder of the world," and while the attribution is debatable, the math is not. The difference between simple interest (returns on your original investment only) and compound interest (returns on your investment plus accumulated returns) becomes enormous over long time horizons.

The basic future value formula for a lump sum investment is:.

For example, $10,000 invested at 8% for 20 years:.

FV = $10,000 x (1.08)^20 = $10,000 x 4.661 = $46,610.

In a recent development, the table reveals two critical insights. First, small differences in return rates produce massive differences over long periods — $10,000 at 6% grows to $57,435 over 30 years, while the same amount at 10% grows to $174,494. That 4-percentage-point difference triples the outcome. Second, time is the dominant variable. At 8%, your money doubles roughly every 9 years — so 30 years gives you more than three doublings, turning $10,000 into over $100,000.

Most people do not invest a single lump sum and walk away. They invest regularly — monthly or per paycheck — over decades. The future value of a series of regular contributions uses a different formula called the future value of an annuity:.

FV = PMT x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r].

Where PMT is the periodic contribution, r is the periodic rate, and n is the total number of periods.

In practice, you do not need to calculate this by hand. The insight that matters is this: regular contributions are far more powerful than most people realize because each contribution starts its own compounding clock. Your first $500 contribution compounds for the full 30 years, while your 360th contribution (at month 360) compounds for just one month — but together they build wealth that dwarfs a single lump sum.

Industry observers note that A person investing $500 per month at 8% for 30 years accumulates $745,180 — from total contributions of only $180,000. That means $565,180, or 76% of the final balance, came from compound returns rather than your own deposits. This is the engine of wealth building.

According to recent reports, every future value calculation should be done twice — once in nominal terms and once in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. The nominal return is the raw number your investments earn. The real return subtracts inflation, showing you what your money will actually buy.

In a recent development, historically, the S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% nominally and 7% after inflation. The difference matters enormously over long periods:.

In a recent development, that $1.13 million in nominal terms has the purchasing power of roughly $610,000 in today's dollars — still excellent, but nearly half less than the headline number suggests. When planning for FI, always use real returns (6-7%) rather than nominal returns (9-10%) to avoid overestimating what your portfolio will actually support in retirement spending.

Industry observers note that the Rule of 72 is the simplest and most useful mental math tool in investing. Divide 72 by your annual rate of return to estimate how many years it takes for your investment to double:.

This works in reverse too. If you want to know what rate of return you need to double your money in 15 years: 72 / 15 = 4.8%. The Rule of 72 is an approximation — it is most accurate for rates between 5% and 12% — but it is remarkably precise within that range and far faster than pulling out a calculator.

Sources indicate that the FI community uses future value calculations as the backbone of retirement planning. The process works in three steps:.

It has been revealed that the table shows how starting balance and monthly contribution interact. Notice that increasing your monthly contribution from $1,500 to $2,500 (a $1,000 increase) with a $100,000 starting balance cuts 3.5 years off your time to $1 million. This is the savings rate lever in action — the amount you save each month matters more than any other variable you control.

According to recent reports, A common question is whether it is better to invest a lump sum now or spread contributions over time (dollar-cost averaging). The math is clear: lump sum investing wins approximately two-thirds of the time because markets trend upward over the long term. However, dollar-cost averaging reduces the psychological risk of investing a large amount right before a downturn and provides a behavioral advantage that keeps many investors on track. For most FI-seekers, the question is academic — you invest each paycheck as it arrives because you do not have a large lump sum sitting on the sidelines.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Recent findings suggest that when projecting your portfolio growth for retirement planning, use real (inflation-adjusted) returns of 6-7% rather than nominal returns of 9-10%. A $1 million nominal balance in 30 years has the purchasing power of roughly $550,000 in today's dollars at 2% average inflation. Planning with real returns ensures you are targeting a portfolio that can actually support your desired spending level.

Track your actual spending for 3 months and annualize it. Multiply by 25 to get your FI number using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. If you spend $60,000 per year, your FI number is $1,500,000.

Sources indicate that add up all retirement accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), taxable brokerage accounts, and savings. Exclude home equity and non-liquid assets. This is your starting balance for the future value calculation.

Sources indicate that subtract your monthly spending from your monthly after-tax income. Include employer 401(k) match and any other automatic savings. This is your periodic contribution amount for the future value formula.

Use the future value of a lump sum plus annuity formula, or a simple online calculator, to project when your current balance plus monthly contributions will reach your FI number. Use 7% real return (after inflation) for conservative planning.

Test what happens if you increase contributions by $200/month, $500/month, or $1,000/month. Seeing the concrete impact of a savings rate increase — often shaving 2-5 years off your FI timeline — makes the trade-offs tangible and motivating.

Recent findings suggest that for long-term stock market projections, use 7% for inflation-adjusted (real) returns or 10% for nominal returns based on the S&P 500 historical average. For a more conservative estimate, use 6% real. For bond-heavy portfolios, use 3-4% real. Always specify whether you are using nominal or real returns — mixing them up is one of the most common planning mistakes.

It has been revealed that future value calculations show what WOULD happen if returns were constant every year. In reality, markets fluctuate — you might earn 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Over 20-30 year periods, average returns tend to converge toward historical norms, making future value projections reasonably useful for planning. Treat them as directional estimates, not guarantees.

Recent findings suggest that future value asks: "What will $10,000 today be worth in 20 years?" Present value asks the reverse: "What is $50,000 in 20 years worth in today's dollars?" They use the same variables but in opposite directions. Present value is useful for evaluating whether a future payout (like a pension or annuity) is worth the cost today.

The Rule of 72 works for any compounding rate, including inflation. At 3% inflation, prices double every 24 years (72 / 3 = 24). This means $50,000 in annual spending today becomes $100,000 in 24 years in nominal terms — your purchasing power is halved if your income stays flat. This is why investing in assets that outpace inflation is essential.

For FI planning, future value is more intuitive — it tells you what your portfolio will grow to. However, the most practical approach is to calculate future value using real (after-inflation) returns. This effectively gives you a future value stated in today's purchasing power, which is what you actually need to know for spending planning.

It has been revealed that in tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), your investments compound without tax drag, so the standard future value formula works directly. In taxable accounts, capital gains taxes, dividend taxes, and tax-loss harvesting all affect your real return. A rough adjustment is to reduce your assumed return by 0.5-1.0% for taxable accounts to account for ongoing tax drag.

Future value calculations are the most practical tool in the FI planner's toolkit. They turn abstract concepts like compound growth and savings rate into concrete dollar amounts and specific timelines. The key takeaways are straightforward: use 7% real returns for conservative planning, always account for inflation by using real rather than nominal returns, and remember that your monthly contribution rate has a far larger impact on the outcome than chasing an extra point or two of return. The Rule of 72 gives you instant mental math for any investment decision — how long to double, what rate you need, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. Combined with a clear FI number and a disciplined savings rate, future value projections show you exactly when financial independence becomes reality. Run the numbers, test different scenarios, and let the math motivate you to increase that monthly contribution whenever you can.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ten leading designers have unveiled posters that celebrate 10 years of London’s Design Museum in Kensington, which was completed by OMA, Allies and Morrison and John Pawson in 2016.

Originally located in an old 1940s banana warehouse on the south bank of the River Thames, the Design Museum opened at its current site in Kensington, west London, on 24 November 2016.

To mark this 10-year anniversary, the museum asked 10 international designers to create posters for the occasion.

The lineup includes British graphic designer Margaret Calvert, who is known for creating the seminal 1960s Motorway and Transport typefaces with fellow British designer Jock Kinneir.

The hugely popular typefaces were invented to clarify the UK’s road signs and are still used today.

Calvert designed a subtle road sign-style poster for the Design Museum’s anniversary, depicting a fork in the road between Kensington and Shad Thames, where the original museum stood between 1989 and 2016.

Former Apple designer Jony Ive also conceived a poster in collaboration with his studio LoveFrom, which he founded with Australian practitioner Marc Newson in 2019 after his departure from the technology brand.

Ive and LoveFrom‘s poster features a minimalist grey and white design composed of two understated shapes that resemble the number 10.

American filmmaker Tim Burton is also among the lineup and applied his trademark playful drawings to a poster illustrated with two characters sitting atop the number 10.

Burton’s extensive portfolio was on display at the Design Museum in 2024, charting 50 years of his cinematic career.

Dutch industrial designer Hella Jongerius, meanwhile, created a poster depicting a colourful woven tapestry in a nod to her work, which typically blends contemporary technology with traditional crafts.

The other six designers who make up the lineup are London studio A Practice for Everyday Life, Brazilian graphic designer Marina Willer, British fashion designer Paul Smith and British designers Sebastian Conran, Simone Brewster and Tom Dixon.

The Kensington Design Museum is located within the former Commonwealth Institute building.

Dutch architecture practice OMA worked alongside London office Allies and Morrison to restore the shell of the Grade II*-listed building, while British designer Pawson conceived the museum’s interiors.

Images courtesy of Design Museum.

It's at the moment got a small saving of $20 at Amazon.

Furniture designers contend with their personal experiences living in Newly introduced York City through the objects in our most recent roundup.

New York, New York has inspired filmmakers, writers and artists to make work since the city’s inception, and for designers, it’s no different.

The furniture and objects below explore aspects of moving to or living in Newly introduced York City, whether it’s the difficulty of maintaining a career and community, the dissonance of missing home, the architecture, or dead, smooshed rats on the daily commute.

In many cases, the collections reflect on the designer’s own identities and heritages.

These include pieces by Kim Mupungilaï, Rafael Prieto and studio Tian & Teague, all of whom have lived or passed through Newly introduced York during their practice.

Read on below to see how the metropolis has shaped their work.

What Still Holds, by Bechara Maalouf.

Bechara Maalouf created a series of lamps made out of wooden beams from Lower East Side buildings and intricate screens informed by the window guards at his family home in Lebanon.

The series, first displayed during NYC design week 2026 in May, merged Maalouf’s two homes as the designer grappled with the impacts of Israel’s ground invasion of Lebanon from afar.

Find out more about What Still Holds ›.

Pax New Yorkea, by Massimiliano Malagò.

Designer Massimiliano Malagò created an acrylic chair, covered in his own writings, that explores the challenges of maintaining a life in New York City.

“For me, this was making an object that is incredibly luxurious, incredibly grand, but it’s actually talking about something quite common and sometimes quite sad, because the hardships that people go through to stay in the city are just difficult,” he told Dezeen.

Find out more about Pax Upcoming Yorkea ›.

Los Angeles and Lisbon studio Tian & Teague created the NYC Series based on their own time living in Fresh York and some of the jarring aspects residents become accustomed to.

The collection, which includes a flattened-rat rug, came about from things seen on the studio founders’ daily commute.

Find out more about NYC Series ›.

White Picket Chair, by Han Seungmin.

Newly introduced York-based designer Han Seungmin created this chair using modular components from the metallic fences found throughout Brooklyn.

First mass-produced in China in the 1980s, the fences are often used in Asian communities around the boroughs, and Han challenged “the idyllic image of the ‘American Dream’ from an immigrant perspective” through the piece.

Find out more about White Picket Chair ›.

HUE/AM/I-HUE/I/AM, by Kim Mupungilaï.

Belgian interior designer Kim Mupungilaï was prompted to design this collection of wood and fibre furniture after a 2018 visit to New York that inspired her to explore her half-Belgian, half-Congolese roots.

“I just started thinking about my own cultural landscape and background and upbringing and wanted to dig deeper,” Mupungilaï told Dezeen.

Find out more about HUE/AM/I-HUE/I/AM ›.

The City Block, by Micah Rosenblatt.

Metalworker and designer Micah Rosenblatt looked to Upcoming York City’s historic architecture for his The City Block collection, which features thin, contemporary lines and geometric elements.

“[The expressions] are based on the cityscape and my relationship to it,” Rosenblatt told Dezeen. “It’s the forms that you would look out and see on your horizon via whatever time period you’re in.”.

Find out more about The City Block ›.

All Other Passports, by Julio Torres and Sabai.

Comedian and actor Julio Torres worked with furniture manufacturer Sabai to create his first furniture collection, All Other Passports, debuted during NYC design week 2026.

The collection is influenced by literal and figurative aspects of Torres’ move to Latest York City from El Salvador, such as a curtain motif pulled from JFK‘s international Terminal 4.

Find out more about All Other Passports ›.

For The Future of the Past, by Rafael Prieto.

Designer Rafael Prieto integrated building fragments into several furniture pieces for an exhibition at Emma Scully Gallery earlier this year.

Prieto sourced the cast-offs, including pieces of a cornice, from a facade being demolished across the street from his Tribeca studio, which he had become “deeply interested” in.

Find out more about For The Future of the Past ›.

Your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:.

Recent findings suggest that 4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. According to recent reports, 4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Recent findings suggest that heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

In a recent development, protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Industry observers note that cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai.

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Sources indicate that regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Recent findings suggest that washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.
  • Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.
